To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transitional justice initiatives in Peru were gender blind and that the transitional justice mechanisms in Peru were not designed in ways that were sensitive to the gendered nature of the violence that occurred in Peru.

transitional justice mechanisms have not been gender-sensitive and, in fact, have been gender-blind in Peru, that this has been due to a combination of factors including lack of knowledge about women’s experiences of the conflict and a limited understanding of gender issues in the country, and that this is problematic for women victims and their communities.

the transitional justice mechanisms in Peru were designed to be gender-neutral and that the mechanisms have not been effective in addressing the specific needs and interests of women victims of violence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the Peruvian state can be held accountable to women and other groups excluded from its transitional justice initiatives.
how transitional justice initiatives in Peru have been shaped by the gender, racial, ethnic, and class dynamics that have historically marginalized the country's indigenous and poor majority.
the question of whether it is possible to develop a gendered transitional justice framework that is both inclusive and transformative, and how such a framework would look.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

engendering transitional mechanisms in Peru is possible, but only if transitional justice actors and their funders and supporters are willing to challenge and transcend the limits of the current framework.
transitional justice mechanisms have been insufficiently attentive to gender, class and racial inequalities.
engendering transitional mechanisms is not only desirable but also possible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transitional justice process in Peru has not been successful in engendering justice for women.

we have been trying to show the ways in which transitional justice mechanisms are gendered, and the ways in which they are also gendered in ways that are not only problematic but also potentially productive for social change.

the Peruvian case demonstrates the need to move away from a focus on individual victimhood and to instead consider the structural causes of gendered violence, and the structural inequalities that make women more vulnerable to such violence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while there are some important gains, there is still much to be done in terms of engendering the Peruvian transitional justice framework.
transitional justice initiatives must go beyond the liberal paradigm to address the structural violence of the state and its role in perpetuating inequality.
the transitional justice mandate must be expanded to include the full range of women's experiences of violence and the structural conditions that make them vulnerable to violence.
